newsitem.title: USA: USDA seen raising corn, soy production estimates.
newsitem.headline: USDA seen raising corn, soy production estimates.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department will likely raise its U.S. corn and soybean production figures in the November crop report but year-end soybean stocks will remain tight, analysts said.
"You've got (soybean) demand improving to the point that you've got to increase the crop or you have to lower the carry," said Steve Freed, analyst with ADM Investor Services.
A Reuter survey of analysts produced an average corn production estimate of 9.145 billion bushels and soybean output of 2.376 billion bushels.
USDA in October pegged U.S. corn output at 9.012 billion bushels and soybeans at 2.346 billion bushels. The November crop report is due on Tuesday at 0730 CST/1330 GMT.
Analysts noted weekly soybean exports were at a record pace in October and soybean meal crushing rates were also at historical highs.
"I think USDA's (usage) numbers are way too low on beans," said Mickey Luth, analyst with The LaiFa Group. "They may revise the crush up some."
Luth estimated corn output at 9.107 billion bushels and soybean production at 2.377 billion.
USDA in October estimated crush usage at 1.375 billion bushels and export demand at 850 million bushels. USDA also put ending soybean stocks at 195 million bushels.
Luth said USDA needed to increase its crush usage figures by 50 million bushels to 1.425 billion bushels.
If usage figures in Tuesday's report increase by more than the production estimate, ending stocks will drop to below 195 million bushels which would be construed as bullish, said ADM's Freed.
"Any (ending stocks) number below 180 (million bushels) would be significant for the market," he said.

Analysts' corn production estimates were also higher than USDA's October projection. Several analysts pointed to weather patterns in September and October which were conducive to development of late planted corn and noted most areas of the U.S. Midwest escaped an early frost.

"I've been amazed at how well this crop has come along given the late planting and all the problems during the growing season," said Marty Foreman, analyst with Agrivisor Services in Bloomington, Ill.
He estimated corn production at 9.236 billion bushels and soybean output at 2.357 billion.
But others thought stories of surprisingly high yields could be overstated.
Doug Hjort, president of Hjort Associates, suggested that crop conditions were too variable in key states like Illinois to draw conclusions from scattered reports of high yields.

"You hear people saying yields were better than expected, but they expected 100 (bushels per acre)," he said. "They came up with 130 (bushels) and that's considered good for an area that typically yields 160."
Hjort pegged corn production at 8.980 billion bushels and soybean output at 2.306 billion.
